notes.text: And the multitude of them that believed — Every individual person were of one heart and one soul - Their love, their hopes, their passions joined: and not so much as one - In so great a multitude: this was a necessary consequence of that union of heart; said that aught of the things which he had was his own - It is impossible any one should, while all were of one soul. So long as that truly Christian love continued, they could not but have all things common.
And great grace — A large measure of the inward power of the Holy Ghost, was upon them all - Directing all their thoughts, words, and actions.

For neither was there any one among them that wanted — We may observe, this is added as the proof that great grace was upon them all. And it was the immediate, necessary consequence of it: yea, and must be to the end of the world. In all ages and nations, the same cause, the same degree of grace, could not but in like circumstances produce the same effect. For whosoever were possessors of houses and lands sold them - Not that there was any particular command for this; but there was great grace and great love: of which this was the natural fruit.
And distribution was made — At first by the apostles themselves, afterward by them whom they appointed.

glossa.text: *There was one heart.* They who had left the world did not, glorying in the nobility of their race, prefer themselves to others, but, as brought forth from the bowels of one and the same mother the Church, rejoiced in the same love of brotherhood. *Neither did any one of them.* The virtues which the just possess they judge to be not their own, but of those to whose profit they dispense them. *Common.* In Greek κοῖνα· whence coenobites, that is, those living in common. Coenobia are their dwellings.

*The apostles gave.* He distinguishes the order of the teachers and of the hearers. For the multitude of believers, temporal things being despised, were joined to one another by the bond of charity. But the apostles, shining with power, set forth the mysteries of Christ.

notes.text: Ointment — It is no less grateful and refreshing than that oil which was poured forth upon Aaron's head at the time of his consecration to the priestly office. Skirts - Not to the lower skirt or bottom of his sacerdotal garment, but to the upper skirt of it, or the mouth of it, as the Hebrew word properly signifies.

Zion — It is as desirable as the dew which falls upon mount Hermon, nay, as desirable as that heavenly dew of God's ordinances and graces which he hath commanded to fall upon the mountains of Zion and Moriah, and others which are round about Jerusalem. There - Where brethren live in peace and unity. In this Psalm the priests or Levites who watched all night in the temple, exhort one another, and pray for one another, ver. 1-3. A song of degrees.

glossa.text: *A canticle of degrees.* ((ID.)) The fourteenth degree: charity, which makes brethren to dwell in one, whence blessing and life. *Behold how good.* And this psalm is an atom, etc., *as far as* here therefore the just man, rejoicing over the dwelling together of brethren, says: *Behold how. Behold how.* ((AUG.)) That verse, most famous in the whole world, has as the trumpet of the Holy Ghost gathered together them that were divided: it has brought forth very many monasteries. ((CASS.)) *Behold.* As though more were set forth by the showing than could be unfolded by the tongue. *To dwell in one.* ((AUG.)) This concerning all Christians, but it properly befits monasteries, from which nevertheless the blessing comes down to the rest, as also to those brethren of Judaea, of whom it is said: *They had one heart,* and *one soul.*

*As the ointment.* ((THEOD.)) The priestly oil, etc., *as far as* it perfects the odour of perfect virtue. *The beard.* ((AUG.)) Behold the determination, that is, upon the apostles and the other primitive saints, who first strove in faith, but could not be overcome, because they had already gone before the head that had suffered *praecesserunt*; read *praecesserat*, "the head had gone before". *Aaron.* The priest who offered up himself, etc., *as far as* but they could not be overcome. From them. *To the skirt.* ((CASS.)) Or by the *skirt,* which is the edge of the garment, etc., *as far as* the profit of concord reaches even to them that are subject.

*As the dew.* ((ID.)) *Dew* is thin water, whence the earth brings forth, and it signifies grace, whereby sinners are converted. *Hermon.* ((AUG.)) According to the letter a mountain beyond Jordan, etc., *as far as* the rest are taken up, who are *in one* in heart.

notes.text: Of communion with the Father, i. 5-10

Of communion with the Son, ii. 1-12 With a distinct application to fathers, young men, and little children, 13-27 Whereto is annexed an exhortation to abide in him, 28- iii. 1-24 That the fruit of his manifestation in the flesh may extend to his manifestation in glory.

Of the confirmation and fruit of this abiding through the Spirit, iv. 1-21 II. Conjointly, Of the testimony of the Father, and Son, and Spirit: on which faith in Christ, the being born of God, love to God and his children, the keeping his commandments and victory over the world, are founded, v. 1-12 The parts frequently begin and end alike. Sometimes there is an allusion in a preceding part, and a recapitulation in the subsequent. Each part treats of a benefit from God, and the duty of the faithful derived therefrom by the most natural inferences. 1st JOHN

That your joy may be full — So our Lord also, John xv, 11; xvi, 22. There is a joy of hope, a joy of faith, and a joy of love. Here the joy of faith is directly intended. It is a concise expression. Your joy - That is, your faith and the joy arising from it: but it likewise implies the joy of hope and love.

And this is the sum of the message which we have heard of him — The Son of God. That God is light - The light of wisdom, love, holiness, glory. What light is to the natural eye, that God is to the spiritual eye. And in him is no darkness at all - No contrary principle. He is pure, unmixed light.

If we say — Either with our tongue, or in our heart, if we endeavour to persuade either ourselves or others. We have fellowship with him, while we walk, either inwardly or outwardly, in darkness - In sin of any kind. We do not the truth - Our actions prove, that the truth is not in us.

But if we walk in the light — In all holiness. As God is (a deeper word than walk, and more worthy of God) in the light, then we may truly say, we have fellowship one with another - We who have seen, and you who have not seen, do alike enjoy that fellowship with God. The imitation of God being the only sure proof of our having fellowship with him. And the blood of Jesus Christ his Son - With the grace purchased thereby. Cleanseth us from all sin - Both original and actual, taking away all the guilt and all the power.

If we say — Any child of man, before his blood has cleansed us. We have no sin - To be cleansed from, instead of confessing our sins, 1 John i, 9, the truth is not in us - Neither in our mouth nor in our heart.

But if with a penitent and believing heart, we confess our sins, he is faithful — Because he had promised this blessing, by the unanimous voice of all his prophets. Just - Surely then he will punish: no; for this very reason he will pardon. This may seem strange; but upon the evangelical principle of atonement and redemption, it is undoubtedly true; because, when the debt is paid, or the purchase made, it is the part of equity to cancel the bond, and consign over the purchased possession. Both to forgive us our sins - To take away all the guilt of them. And to cleanse us from all unrighteousness - To purify our souls from every kind and every degree of it.

Yet still we are to retain, even to our lives' end, a deep sense of our past sins. Still if we say, we have not sinned, we make him a liar — Who saith, all have sinned. And his word is not in us - We do not receive it; we give it no place in our hearts.

My beloved children — So the apostle frequently addresses the whole body of Christians. It is a term of tenderness and endearment, used by our Lord himself to his disciples, John xiii, 33. And perhaps many to whom St. John now wrote were converted by his ministry. It is a different word from that which is translated "little children," in several parts of the epistle, to distinguish it from which, it is here rendered beloved children. I write these things to you, that ye may not sin - Thus he guards them beforehand against abusing the doctrine of reconciliation. All the words, institutions, and judgments of God are levelled against sin, either that it may not be committed, or that it may be abolished. But if any one sin - Let him not lie in sin, despairing of help. We have an advocate - We have for our advocate, not a mean person, but him of whom it was said, "This is my beloved son." Not a guilty person, who stands in need of pardon for himself; but Jesus Christ the righteous; not a mere petitioner, who relies purely upon liberality, but one that has merited, fully merited, whatever he asks.

And he is the propitiation — The atoning sacrifice by which the wrath of God is appeased. For our sins - Who believe. And not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world - Just as wide as sin extends, the propitiation extends also.

glossa.text: *That which was from the beginning.* In the nature, or the true being, of the Godhead, *which we have heard,* through the law and the prophets, *which we have seen,* coming as man in a manner perceptible to the senses, *which we have looked upon,* discerning the Godhead in the man, *and hands have handled, of the Word of life:* not agreeing by chance with him who was seen in the flesh, but with much handling bringing forward the Scriptures as testimony concerning the Word himself. What a man has seen he can announce to others, what he has at some time perfectly beheld he cannot unfold in words.

*We have seen* and are witnesses. We have seen, and by announcing to unbelievers we have been made martyrs. *We declare unto you.* Thus we have heard through them, but we have not seen, yet we are not less blessed than they, because it is written: *Blessed are they that have not seen and have believed ((Luc. XXIV))*.

*And this is the declaration.* Why was the Word made flesh? what new thing did he bring to the world? Why did he come to suffer? It was not in vain, see what he willed to teach, *that God is light.* By this sentence he shows the excellence of the divine purity, which we are bidden to imitate. Hence the Manichaeans are refuted, who say that the nature of God was conquered in war by the prince of darkness and corrupted. *We declare,* etc. We have applied ourselves: unto light, light has shone upon us. We were darkness, now through the light we are light, and we enlighten others, while we announce that sins are forgiven and darkness driven out.

*If we shall say.* Thus far the commendation of the epistle; here he shows in what manner charity is to be held. *And in darkness,* etc. Those who persist in sins, and who darken others, are not counted among his members; whence: *What concord hath Christ with Belial? what fellowship hath light with darkness? ((II Cor. VI.))*

*But if in the light.* We are clean, if we walk in the light, but yet we ought not to think that we can, so long as we live, be wholly cleansed from sins. *As he also is,* etc. God is said to be in the light, because the highest goodness does not find where it may advance, man walks in the light, because by works of the virtues he advances to better things.

*If we shall say,* etc. Those also have not charity who, being proud of their merits, say that they are clean. *We have.* He does not say, *we had:* lest perchance it should seem to have been said of things past.
*That he may forgive us sins.* Those things in us which are graver, he calls sins, but the lesser, he calls iniquity.

*We make him a liar.* God alone is truthful of himself: man is truthful from God, of himself a liar. It is impossible that any saint should at some time not fall into the least sins. Nor do they cease to be just, because with God's help they rise again the more quickly.

*My little children, these things I write,* etc. Lest you take up an evil security, hearing that you are cleansed by God, but that you may have a profitable fear. *If any man shall have sinned.* If out of human frailty you cannot beware of all vices, give diligence that you beware at least of the greater and the more open ones, that temptation may not take hold of you except such as is human. But if anyone shall have fallen even after my admonition, let him not despair. *We have an advocate.* He is not an advocate save to those who call upon him. Let sins displease thee, cry out: and he both hears and sets free. *Jesus Christ the just.* A just advocate does not undertake unjust causes, yet he will defend us as just in the judgment, if we now accuse ourselves as unjust.

notes.text: Mark xvi, 14 Luke xxiv, 36.

Peace be unto you — This is the foundation of the mission of a true Gospel minister, peace in his own soul, 2 Cor. iv, 1. As the Father hath sent me, so send I you - Christ was the apostle of the Father, Heb. iii, 1. Peter and the rest, the apostles of Christ.

He breathed on them — New life and vigour, and saith, as ye receive this breath out of my mouth, so receive ye the Spirit out of my fulness: the Holy Ghost influencing you in a peculiar manner, to fit you for your great embassy. This was an earnest of pentecost.

Whosoever sins ye remit — (According to the tenor of the Gospel, that is, supposing them to repent and believe) they are remitted, and whosoever sins ye retain (supposing them to remain impenitent) they are retained. So far is plain. But here arises a difficulty. Are not the sins of one who truly repents, and unfeignedly believes in Christ, remitted, without sacerdotal absolution? And are not the sins of one who does not repent or believe, retained even with it? What then does this commission imply? Can it imply any more than,

1. A power of declaring with authority the Christian terms of pardon; whose sins are remitted and whose retained? As in our daily form of absolution; and

2. A power of inflicting and remitting ecclesiastical censures? That is, of excluding from, and re-admitting into, a Christian congregation.
After eight days — On the next Sunday.

And Thomas said, My Lord and my God — The disciples had said, We have seen the Lord. Thomas now not only acknowledges him to be the Lord, as he had done before, and to be risen, as his fellow disciples had affirmed, but also confesses his Godhead, and that more explicitly than any other had yet done. And all this he did without putting his hand upon his side.
Jesus wrought many miracles, which are not written in this book — Of St. John, nor indeed of the other evangelists.
But these things are written that ye may believe — That ye may be confirmed in believing. Faith cometh sometimes by reading; though ordinarily by hearing.

glossa.text: *When therefore,* etc. This was done on the very day of the resurrection, on which Jesus appeared five times. First to Mary Magdalene, secondly to the same woman running with the others who wished to announce it to the disciples, thirdly to Peter, fourthly to Cleophas and his companion, fifthly to the disciples, the doors being shut, the two aforesaid having now returned.

*He shewed them his hands and his side.* After the resurrection the Lord showed in his body two contrary things: both what was palpable, of the same nature, that he might form them to faith, and what was incorruptible, of another glory, that he might invite them to the reward.

*He said therefore to them again. Peace be to you,* etc. He offers peace, who came for the sake of peace; he repeats it, that he may show that through his blood the things that are in heaven and the things that are on earth have been made peaceful.
*Receive ye the Holy Ghost. ((AUG.))* On earth the spirit is given that the neighbour may be loved; from heaven the Spirit is given that God may be loved.

*Whose sins you shall forgive.* Behold charity, which is poured into their hearts through the Holy Ghost. He forgives the sins of those who are partakers of him; of those who are not, he retains them. And therefore after he had said: *Receive ye the Holy Ghost,* he immediately subjoined: *Whose sins you shall forgive.*

*Now Thomas, one.* Not by chance, but by divine disposition was Thomas absent, and he did not believe what he heard; whence the Lord offered himself to him to be handled, because by his doubting, and by the proof made to him, it is now left to no one to doubt. *Who is called Didymus.* Didymus, that is, twin, because Thomas is doubtful; that is, an abyss: because by doubting he knew more deeply.
*He answered.* He was seeing and touching the man, and above this he believed him God, doubt being now removed, and he confessed him whom he did not see.

*Because thou hast seen me, Thomas, thou hast believed.* He does not say, thou hast touched, but, thou hast seen: because sight is in a manner the general sense, which is wont to be said of the other four. Perhaps he did not dare to touch; but by looking only, or even by touching, he believes.

*Blessed.* He commends the faith of the Gentiles, but he uses the past tense, as one who knew that what was to come was already done in his own predestination.

echoes.text: However there shall be no poor with you (for Yahweh will surely bless you in the land which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance to possess it)
echoes.note: Verse 34, 'neither was there among them any who lacked,' closely echoes Deut 15:4 LXX, 'there shall be no poor/needy among you,' the Deuteronomic ideal of the covenant community in which God's blessing eliminates poverty. Luke presents the Jerusalem community's common purse as the fulfillment of this Torah promise — strong thematic coherence and notable verbal overlap on 'no one lacked / no poor.'

echoes.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: The believers being 'of one heart and soul' (v.32) faintly recalls the Shema's 'with all your heart and with all your soul' (Deut 6:5); here the heart-and-soul language describes communal unity rather than love of God. A lexical resonance only, low and contested.

echoes.text: and I will give them one heart and one way, that they may fear me forever, for their good, and of their children after them:
echoes.note: 'One heart and one soul' (v.32) may echo the new-covenant promise of Jer 32:39 (LXX 39:39), 'I will give them one heart and one way,' where God grants the restored people a unified heart. The Spirit-given unity of the believers coheres with this restoration promise. Low, contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Aaron, “You shall have no inheritance in their land, neither shall you have any portion among them. I am your portion and your inheritance among the children of Israel.
echoes.note: The closing note that Barnabas, 'a Levite' (v.36), sold his field and laid the proceeds at the apostles' feet plays ironically against Num 18:20, where Levites were to have no landed inheritance because the LORD was their portion. Barnabas's divestment of a field embodies that Levitical landlessness in the new community. Typological/ironic, no verbal borrowing.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.id: The City of David and Old City, on the spurs above the Kidron Valley, c. 50 km from the Mediterranean. Pre-Israelite Jebus; named here as the seat of Adoni-Zedek, leader of the southern coalition.

places.name: Nazareth
places.id: Modern en-Nasira / Nazareth in Lower Galilee, c. 30 km west of the Sea of Galilee. A village of perhaps 200-400 in the early first century, identified through continuous habitation, tomb evidence, and the third-century Caesarea inscription naming it as a priestly course settlement.

places.name: Cyprus
places.id: The third-largest Mediterranean island, a Roman senatorial province since 22 B.C. with capital at Paphos. Home of Barnabas (Acts 4:36), site of Paul and Barnabas's first missionary stop (Acts 13:4-12). Pin sits in the central Troodos range; the cities (Salamis, Paphos, Citium) appear later in the book.

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
echoes.note: The opening phrase 'that which was from the beginning' deliberately echoes the Septuagint's 'en arche' of Genesis 1:1. The author frames the proclamation in cosmogonic terms, locating the Word of life at the primordial beginning of all things.

echoes.text: By Yahweh’s word, the heavens were made; all their army by the breath of his mouth.
echoes.note: 'By the word of the LORD the heavens were made' supplies the background for a life-giving creative word. The Word of life that was from the beginning draws on the tradition of God's word as the agent of creation and vivification.

echoes.text: “Yahweh possessed me in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old. I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth existed.
echoes.note: Personified Wisdom, 'possessed from the beginning, before the earth was,' provides a conceptual matrix for a pre-existent Word that was from the beginning with the Father. The 1 John prologue shares the sapiential vocabulary of primordial origin.

echoes.text: God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
echoes.note: The creative divine word that calls light into being ('Let there be light') resonates faintly with the 'Word of life' that is manifested. The juxtaposition of beginning, word, and life recalls the spoken creation of Genesis.

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: The manifested 'life' that the witnesses heard, saw, and touched may recall God breathing the breath of life into the human, the originating gift of life. The link is thematic rather than verbal.

echoes.text: She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her. Happy is everyone who retains her.
echoes.note: Wisdom as a 'tree of life' to those who lay hold of her loosely parallels the 'eternal life' that the witnesses lay hold of and touch with their hands. A faint sapiential resonance.

echoes.text: to love Yahweh your God, to obey his voice, and to cling to him; for he is your life, and the length of your days; that you may dwell in the land which Yahweh swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give them.
echoes.note: The LORD as 'your life and the length of your days' undergirds the Johannine equation of God/Word with life itself. The eternal life that was with the Father echoes the covenantal life found in God.

echoes.text: For she is a breath of the power of God, And a clear effluence of the glory of the Almighty; Therefore can nothing defiled find entrance into her. For she is an effulgence from everlasting light, And an unspotted mirror of the working of God, And an image of his goodness.
echoes.note: Wisdom as 'a pure emanation' and 'reflection of eternal light' with God supplies a deuterocanonical bridge for the pre-existent life that was with the Father and was manifested. Shares the language of a divine reality made visible.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: Jesus 'breathed on them' and said 'Receive the Holy Spirit' — the verb (enephysesen, LXX of Gen 2:7) directly evokes God breathing the breath of life into Adam's nostrils so he became a living being. John presents the Spirit-impartation as new creation/new Adam; very high Volume given the rare shared verb and high Coherence with the Gospel's creation theology.

echoes.text: Then he said to me, Prophesy to the wind, prophesy, son of man, and tell the wind, Thus says the Lord Yahweh: Come from the four winds, breath, and breathe on these slain, that they may live. So I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up on their feet, an exceedingly great army.
echoes.note: 'Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe on these slain, that they may live' stands behind Jesus breathing Spirit into the disciples after the resurrection. Ezekiel's vivified corpses give the scene its resurrection-and-Spirit valence; high Coherence and shared breath/Spirit (ruach/pneuma) vocabulary reinforce the Genesis 2:7 figure.

echoes.text: ‘Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
echoes.note: The risen Jesus' threefold greeting 'Peace be to you' (20:19,21,26) functions as the eschatological enactment of the Aaronic priestly blessing 'the LORD lift up his countenance on you and give you peace.' Medium Volume (shared 'peace') with strong Coherence as the resurrected high-priestly Lord blesses his gathered people.

echoes.text: I will lay the key of the house of David on his shoulder. He will open, and no one will shut. He will shut, and no one will open.
echoes.note: The authority to forgive or retain sins ('he shall open, and no one shall shut; he shall shut, and no one shall open') parallels the key-of-the-house-of-David grant of binding/loosing power. The remit-or-retain antithesis matches the open/shut structure of the oracle; medium confidence on the structural rather than verbal link.

echoes.text: Because he was ignorant of him that moulded him, And of him that inspired into him an active soul, And breathed into him a vital spirit.
echoes.note: 'He failed to know the one who formed him and inspired him with an active soul and breathed into him a living spirit' restates Gen 2:7 in Second-Temple idiom, evidencing the availability of the breath-of-life motif John reworks. Deuterocanonical witness rather than a direct source.

echoes.text: I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake; and I will not remember your sins.
echoes.note: 'I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake' grounds the forgiveness of sins as a divine prerogative now delegated to the disciples (20:23). Faint background highlighting that sin-forgiveness is God's act, sharpening the Christological claim.

echoes.text: Wake up! Rise up to defend me, my God! My Lord, contend for me!
echoes.note: Thomas' confession 'My Lord and my God!' (20:28) reproduces the psalmist's vocative 'my God and my Lord' (LXX Ps 34:23: ho theos mou kai ho kyrios mou). The unusual paired address gives high Volume; John climaxes the Gospel by directing to Jesus the cry the psalmist directs to YHWH.

echoes.text: But you, Lord, are a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth.
echoes.note: Thomas addresses Jesus with the divine titles 'Lord... God' that the psalter repeatedly couples ('you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious'), reinforcing the deliberate transfer of YHWH-language to the risen Christ. Supporting Recurrence behind the primary Ps 35:23 allusion.

echoes.text: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.
echoes.note: 'Blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed' (20:29) coheres with 'the righteous shall live by his faith,' the OT charter of faith-not-sight. Thematic rather than verbal; faint and one of several wisdom/faith backgrounds.

echoes.text: Yahweh answered me, “Write the vision, and make it plain on tablets, that he who runs may read it. For the vision is yet for the appointed time, and it hurries toward the end, and won’t prove false. Though it takes time, wait for it; because it will surely come. It won’t delay.
echoes.note: 'These are written, that you may believe' enacts the prophetic command 'Write the vision; make it plain... it awaits its appointed time,' grounding the inscribed witness-for-faith in the OT theology of the written vision that calls for belief. Medium Coherence with the Gospel's purpose statement; verbal contact is on the writing-for-faith motif.

echoes.text: “At that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people; and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time your people shall be delivered, everyone who shall be found written in the book. Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt. Those who are wise shall […]
echoes.note: The notion of words 'written in this book' so that the faithful 'may have life' faintly recalls Daniel's sealed book and those 'found written in the book' who awake to everlasting life. Low Volume; offered as a faint life-through-the-book resonance.

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.
echoes.note: The confessional goal 'that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God' draws on the royal-messianic decree 'You are my Son,' the OT title-cluster (Messiah / Son of God) John affirms. Background to the titulature rather than a quotation.

lines: The doors were locked, and we were afraid.
But Jesus came and stood among us.
He showed us his hands and his side.
Peace be with you, he said.
He breathed on us the Holy Spirit.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
Come, let us worship, doubt and all.
My Lord and my God!

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Come in, you who bolted the door against the dark, you who are not sure what you believe this morning.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
He passes through every lock you own and stands in the middle of the room, saying, Peace.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
He holds out his hands; the wounds are still there; touch and see that it is really him.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
Then he leans in close and breathes on you, and the breath is the Spirit, and you are sent.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: The doors are locked; our doubts are real.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
He stands among us: Peace be with you.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
He breathes on us and shows his wounded hands.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
Come, let us answer with Thomas.
My Lord and my God!
